name: Philo Carpenter's Log Drug Store
aka: the log shop beside the Sauganash

documented_range.note: THE END OF THIS RANGE IS THE WEAKEST CLAIM IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS WEAKER THAN HOGAN'S, WHICH IS SAYING SOMETHING. What is attested: Philo Carpenter reached Chicago on 18 July 1832 and opened the town's first drug store in a log building 16 x 20 ft on Lake Street near the river. The range opens on the day he arrived because no source gives the shop a build date and he cannot have opened it earlier. THE PROBLEM IS WHAT HE DID NEXT. In the summer of 1833 Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and 'erected a small store' — carpenter_south_water_store in this dataset — and no source reached says what became of the log shop when he moved his trade into it. So this building is placed in a scene set two years after its proprietor built himself a better one, on nothing but the ordinary continuity argument that a standing building stands until something says otherwise. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS SPECIFIC AND STRONG. Lake Street beside the Sauganash was the most valuable frontage at the forks; a 16 x 20 ft log shop is the smallest building in this dataset; and its one attested occupant demonstrably left it. A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT NARROWS NOTHING HERE. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own advertisement, dated 22 November 1833, offering drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs and also dry groceries, glass and nails — proof that he was trading at Chicago sixteen months after arriving and nineteen months before the scene date, but it gives no address, so it cannot say WHICH of his two buildings he was trading from, and it must not be read as evidence that the log shop survived. GRADE: this record's existence at the scene date is the single most likely thing in this parcel to be wrong. If evidence turns up that the log shop came down or was moved before July 1835 it belongs in data/exclusions.json and this record leaves the scene.

position.symbolic_location: Lake Street near the river, on the south side, immediately east of and against the Sauganash Hotel — the source says immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar.
position.note: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING RATHER THAN AGAINST A STREET. The sources give a relation, not an address: a log building on Lake Street near the river, 'immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar' (docs/research/03-structures-north.md § 1). So this position is derived from data/structures/sauganash_hotel.json's own placement and inherits every uncertainty in it. THE SAUGANASH'S PLACEMENT, RESTATED SO THIS RECORD CAN BE RE-DERIVED: the Sauganash stands at the south-east corner of Lake and Market, its frame_1831 footprint origin at EPSG:26916 E 447174.1, N 4637265.2, 12 m wide and 8 m deep with a facade bearing of 0, so its north face is on the Lake Street frontage at N 4637273.2 and its east face at E 447186.1. THIS SHOP IS SET HARD AGAINST THAT EAST FACE, its own west wall on E 447186.1 and its north face on the same Lake Street frontage, which is what 'immediately adjacent' means and is why the two footprints touch. WHICH SIDE THE BAR WAS ON IS NOT ATTESTED and the east side is chosen by elimination: the Sauganash's west face stands on the Market Street frontage, so there is no room for a shop there, and the two retrospective depictions the project holds put the surviving 1829 log wing on the building's left front, which is the Market side. If the public bar was in fact on the west or the river side, this shop is on the wrong flank and moves about 20 m. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, the georeference's residual (data/datum.json, 17.5 m RMS), carried in from the Sauganash rather than added to. Facade bearing 0, north onto Lake Street, and the 20 ft dimension is set along the street with the 16 ft as the depth — the same convention hogan_store's record argues for and, like it, an inference rather than evidence. Turning the shop through 90 degrees would make it a 16 ft frontage 20 ft deep, and nothing decides.

derivation.reason: This placement predates the derivation module. Its provenance and reasoning are recorded in position.note, but no machine-checkable derivation block has been authored for it yet.

footprint.note: THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEHOLDER, after Hogan's store. Andreas gives the size: a 16 x 20 ft log building. 16 x 20 ft is 4.877 x 6.096 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: '16 x 20' is a rectangle in any reading and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a counter, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with a shed on the back. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs. This is the smallest building in the dataset — 30 square metres, a single pen — and that is worth reading twice: Chicago's first drug store was a room.

construction.note: Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1832 and what the source names.

stories.note: Not stated. A 16 x 20 ft single-pen log building is single-storey by type, and a two-storey building on that plan would be a tower. Inference from the documented dimensions, which is as close to derivation from evidence as this dataset's storey counts get.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. The same reading and the same number this project gives Hogan's store and the Walker meeting house.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region. A shed roof leaning on the Sauganash's east wall is the one plausible alternative — 'immediately adjacent' could describe a lean-to — and it is recorded here rather than built, because nothing in the sources describes the junction between the two buildings.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested, and nothing describes a stack on this building. One is the minimum for a shop kept through Chicago winters, and a druggist compounding in an unheated room in January is not a thing. The COUNT is the inference; the stack's position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md L26.

phases.change_note: Chicago's first drug store: a 16 x 20 ft log shop on Lake Street beside the Sauganash's bar, opened by Philo Carpenter after he reached the town on 18 July 1832. By the scene date Carpenter has had his own store on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells for two years, and what this building was doing in July 1835 — or whether it was still standing at all — is unattested.

function.note: THE FUNCTION IS DOCUMENTED FOR 1832 AND INFERRED FOR 1835, and the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas has this as Chicago's first drug store from 1832. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 — 'WILL keep constantly on hand a general assortment of DRUGS, MEDICINES, Oils, Paints, Dye-Stuffs &c. &c. ALSO Dry Groceries, Glass, Nails, &c.' — proves the trade was still his in November 1833 but gives no address and therefore cannot say which of his two buildings held it. Since he had built the South Water store by then, the likelier reading is that the drug trade had already moved and this shop was doing something else, or nothing, on 1835-07-01.

occupants.value: unattested at the scene date; Philo Carpenter from 1832
occupants.note: Carpenter is documented as the proprietor from 1832 and as the owner of a different store on South Water from the summer of 1833. NO SOURCE REACHED NAMES ANYONE IN THIS BUILDING IN 1835. The record says so rather than carrying Carpenter forward into a building he had demonstrably moved out of.

research_note: A RARE COMBINATION AND THE REASON THIS RECORD IS WORTH HAVING: THE FOOTPRINT IS EVIDENCE AND THE EXISTENCE IS NOT. Andreas gives the dimensions — 16 x 20 ft, log, Lake Street near the river — which makes this only the second footprint in the dataset that is not a placeholder, after Hogan's store. Everything about whether it was still there on 1835-07-01 is argued on documented_range and it is argued against: Carpenter built himself a store on South Water in the summer of 1833 and nothing follows the log shop after that. THE CONTEMPORARY ADVERTISEMENT DOES NOT RESCUE IT. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own notice, dated 22 November 1833, and it is genuine primary evidence that he was trading — but it carries no address, it is nineteen months before the scene date, and by then he already had two premises. Treating it as evidence that the log shop stood would be exactly the move this project's confidence model exists to prevent. THE POSITION IS DERIVED FROM ANOTHER RECORD, which is a first here: the source gives a relation ('immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar') and not an address, so this shop is set hard against the Sauganash's east wall and inherits that building's placement and its uncertainty. The two footprints touch, deliberately. WHAT WOULD SETTLE ANY OF IT: the individual building rectangles on Hathaway 1834 or Wright 1834 at the Lake and Market corner, which would show whether one building or two stood on that frontage; the Chicago Democrat for 1834-35, where an address in one of Carpenter's later advertisements would place his trade; or the DRLOIH treatment of Carpenter, cited in this project's north dossier and not yet held as a source record. See docs/RESEARCH/philo_carpenter_log_shop.md.
